content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a flexible online predictive distribution update approach, that is, predicting the distribution of the new data given the existing data. Their work is in line with works such as (Hahn 2018) on "recursive Bayesian predictive distribution" approximation. 
The main contribution is the use of Dirichlet process mixture model with Autoregressive likelihood model and GP priors. They have also studied the use of Autoregressive neural nets for non-smooth data distributions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
* Strength:
1. The proposed Autoregressive Recursive Bayesian Predictive (AR-BP) is quite flexible and according to their reported results performs well on small/moderate size datasets. 
2. Manual hyper-parameter tuning is not required

Weakness:
1. A comparative computation time is missing. An elementary time analysis is provided in the supplementary material but the algorithm is not compared with the existing methods. 
2. The performance of the presented AR-BP on large datasets is not strong.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well written. Though I think some terminology are a bit confusing. For instance, in the Into, it would be clearer to refer to the function f(.) as the "likelihood function" which is more conventional rather than  "sampling distribution".

The quality of the work is high, an interesting problem is tackled which can potentially have many applications. The proposed algorithm is reasonably novel. I have not checked any accompanying code but I believe the results are reproducible and the hyperparameters, and implementation details are spelled out.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Online updating of the predictive probability distribution is an interesting task with many potential applications. 
This work belongs to a line of research that try to tackle this problem and it improves over the existing literature by considering a flexible kernel as well as neural nets. 
My main criticism is due to the lack of a comparative time analysis. 
As far as I can say, the motivation and improvement of  any "Online update of the predictive probability" over the baseline (i.e. recomputing the posterior distributions after new data is given) is saving computations which should show itself in less training time. If that is the case, then providing supporting evidence would add to the value of the work. In the authors can provide such time analysis in the rebuttal, I would be happy to increase my score.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new density estimator that employs kernels with autoregressive structures and base measures constructed by Gaussian processes. I.e. it extends DPMM's model capacity and complexity by adding neural network structures and a more complex dirichlet process.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper proposes an interesting idea to equip DPMM with more flexible structures to accommodate density estimation for more complex data distributions. I like that the high level idea is straightforward and easy to understand.

However, this paper was not written in a very reader-friendly way to present its motivations, detailed methods and intuitions on why we need to incorporate more complex structures given the relative small data size (~10^4-10^5). A motivating example was given on chessboard data but first, I can't tell how the proposed AR-BP, ARnet-BP are significantly better than R-BP and AR, and second, I don't know what these acronyms stand for or any intuitions on why we need new methods.

Aside from writing (which I'll talk more in the "clarity" part), this paper also lacks evidence on empirical results. The datasets being investigated are all small UCI datasets (and a very limited number of them). For the density estimation task, the authors used classification/regression tasks and it's unclear what variables are being used for density estimation (e.g. is it x or (x,y)). The authors proposed several variants of the AR based BP method. Two of them (AR-BP and ARnet-BP) performed somewhat poorly on most of the tasks for density estimation. On supervised learning tasks, the results have more variance. Only NLL was used as the metric for both tasks, though metrics like RMSE or accuracy seem to be more indicative for supervised learning.

It is unclear which of these methods would be  more useful in what scenarios. With such limited empirical results, it is also very difficult to tell if the proposed methods really have any substantial improvements over existing ones, and why that could be the case.

The authors also indicated quite a few times that Bayesian methods work well only when the sample size is small (it probably wasn't mentioned explicitly but that's my impression after reading this work). Meanwhile, the proposed method, while a lot more complex, don't show promise on large dataset as discussed in section 6. The definition of large dataset in this paper is also very much unclear. What's the difference between Small UCI and Benchmark UCI? Is Benchmark UCI considered as large?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This work is promising on novelty but more improvements can be done on other aspects including clarity, quality and reproducibility.

On quality, the proposed method is very complex by design while only works on small datasets. This is counter intuitive. Why do we need more complicated models if we are still in the small data domain? Why doesn't Occam's Razor apply here? Explaining answers to these questions will convince readers more on the quality of this work. In general, I'd suggest not making methods more complicated for simple tasks.

Throughout this paper, it was indicated that Bayesian methods are useful mostly just for small-data problems. What about Bayesian neural net, sparse Gaussian process etc? I understand that the authors are trying to justify that their method is also for small datasets, but I think that "Bayesian methods are useful for small dataset" point could be rephrased by emphasizing why small dataset problems matter. I suggest introducing some examples where the tasks are very important and large scale data is not applicable at all. It's not always clear to modern machine learning audiences why we can't collect more data. And saying something like "Bayesian methods are useful for small dataset" is only going to create more confusion on whether Bayesian methods can work on large datasets or not.

On reproducibility, there are a lot of design choices that need to be made and heuristics have to be adopted to make it work. It's not to say heuristics are bad, but it's difficult to understand how the method can generalize. I briefly took a look at the code and there are so many "magic numbers" (network structure, optimization parameters etc) and given the insufficient empirical results, it is difficult to believe that the method can generalize. But maybe the authors could comment more on this. I'd suggest carrying out sensitivity analyses on those hyperparameters/networks structures, and show more empirical results on more challenging tasks for density estimation and supervised learning (e.g. would image / text classification be applicable?). 

On clarity, here are my comments:
1. A lot of acronyms are not explained until experiments. This makes the introduction very difficult to read.
2. There are unclear assumptions. Below Eq 2, does the independence hold without conditioning on theta? Where was this assumption mentioned?
3. Top of page 3: what's the relation between p(y1, y2) and p_i? Is this C at line 1 the same as the one at line 3? Maybe cite that theorem as a theorem instead of mixing it in the text? 
4. What is x_n in Eq 3?
5. Below Eq 3: how can a function c_n converge to 1?
6. Above Eq 4: ".. propose DPMMs as.." Do you mean "proposed to use DPMMs as"?
7. Since this work also uses GP which has a covariance function, which is also called kernel, I think it would be necessary to state what the authors meant by "kernel" more clearly.
8. Eq 8: is \theta^j a function? In sec 2.2, it was used as parameter in R^d.
9. Inconsistency on citations, e.g. beginning of sec 5.1, some methods have citations, some not.
10. Sec 5.1: "The baselines were hyperparameter tuned over multiple parameters." What does this mean?
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper introduced an interesting method to expand the capacity of DPMM. However, given the issues with quality, clarity and limited empirical evidence, I cannot recommend acceptance at this point.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The author(s) consider the problem of multivariate density estimation, more specifically Bayesian (based) predictive density estimation. The starting point is the approach proposed by Fong et al (2021), considering a Dirichlet Process Mixture Model with factorized Gaussian Kernel and Gaussian base measure for the DP. In the aforementioned paper an updating scheme using copulas were also presented (as standard MCMC methods are overly slow) resulting in a quasi-posterior distribution. In the present paper the authors extend this approach by working with an autoregressive kernel instead of a factorized one and endowing the autoregressive function with a GP prior. This proposed method is clearly more flexible and the authors argue that by using the corresponding copula updating scheme the method is computationally also feasible. This approach provides (amongst others) a data driven bandwidth function in contrast to the deterministic bandwidth of Fong et al (2021). The author(s) also propose a bandwidth function based on AR neural networks. They carry out an extended numerical analysis comparing the proposed methods with several competitors including the base line given in Fong et al (2021). In the supplement they derive the copula based updating scheme. They also discuss extensions to regression and classification.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
General comment: The paper heavily builds on Fong et al (2021), uses it as a starting point both for the methodology and the theory. Nevertheless, the proposed modifications (although AR methods are not uncommon for density estimation) are new, contain technical challanges, and improvements.

Strength:
- sophisticated method, has good performance, usually one of the best in all examples considered in the numerical study
- extensions to other models are discussed
- two methods were considered for bandwidth selection (the second based on AR neural network)
- An extended numerical analysis was carried out, the method was compared with several competitors
- Quite thorough analsys

Weakness:
- The improvement wasn't too big compared to the R-BP method, at least in several of the examples
- The computational time wasn't compared with the R-BP method (I have seen computatinal time measured only in Figure 6, but there only the AR neural and AR methods were compared)
- The choice of the permutation number seems arbitrary in the numerical analysis, i.e. $M=10$ was considered. It should be discussed in more details as it heavily effects the computational time.
- In Table 2, IONO data set the $R-BP$ method was performing substantially better than the more flexible $R_d-BP$ method. How is this possible?
- In the numerical data analysis in the supplement $d=2$ was chosen so it is hard to assess how well the approach performs in larger dimensions. (Although in the main part a larger, but still relatively small dimensional feature space was chosen).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is dense, but this is also due to the format and page limitaiton. Reading the paper Fong et al (2021) helps in understanding the scope and preliminary results better. Neverthelss, the quality of the writing is overal good, beside the quite-heavy technical nature it is relatively well readable. There are some typos, (e.g. in (3) the index is $i$ not $n$, similarly in the 2nd line of section 2.2.), but nothing major.
content.summary_of_the_review: All in all, I think it is an ok contribution to the conference. A nice result, it won't change the world, but it is also not straightforward. The paper has shortcomings, which should be addressed, but in general it is a natural and potentially useful extension of an earlier, impactful approach. The method seems to have good practical performance and can be extended to other models as well (the authors discuss regression and classification).
